findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled
findings.body: All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their timeout context from the incoming request `ctx`. As soon as the HTTP handler returns (which happens immediately, since the goroutine is fired and the response is returned), the apiserver cancels the request context, which cancels the derived child context. The legacy write will then frequently fail with `context canceled` instead of running for its intended 10s budget, silently losing the legacy copy of the data. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration in Create and Update
findings.body: On the storage error path of Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The failing call was to unified storage, so this inflates the legacy error/duration metric and leaves storage failures unrecorded, making the mode-3 dashboards misleading.

findings.title: DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy call as storage duration
findings.body: Inside the async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine the result is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This attributes legacy latency/errors to the storage metric; it should be `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection failures will therefore never show up in the legacy error metric.

findings.title: Object name used as metric label in Delete success path
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Since names are unbounded (one per resource), this creates an unbounded number of Prometheus label values, causing cardinality explosion / memory growth in the metrics registry, and it also breaks comparability with the other recorded durations.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base logger rather than `log`, so downstream code reading the logger from the context loses the name/kind/method values that were just attached. Every other method in the file passes `log`.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests race with the async legacy goroutine and never assert it ran
findings.body: The implementation now performs the legacy write in a goroutine, but the tests return as soon as the synchronous call completes. The same `*mock.Mock` is shared between the legacy and storage mocks, so the goroutine calls `m.Called(...)` concurrently with (or after) the test's assertions — a data race that `-race` will flag, and possibly a call into a `t` that has already finished. Additionally no test asserts that the legacy store was actually written to (e.g. via `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting), so the core behaviour of mode 3 is untested. The tests need synchronization (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) before asserting.

findings.title: Legacy Create is given the pre-create object which storage may have mutated
findings.body: The goroutine passes the original `obj` to `d.Legacy.Create`. `d.Storage.Create` may have mutated `obj` in place (resourceVersion, UID, generated name) or the legacy store may generate a different name/UID, so the two stores can diverge in identity — exactly what mode 3's background legacy write is meant to prevent. Consider passing the returned `created` object (as mode 2's update path did with `updateWrapper`).

findings.title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry added
findings.body: `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` is added at line 408 while the identical line already exists a few lines above. These go.work.sum additions look like unrelated/accidental churn for a dual-writer change and should be dropped or regenerated.
